title: E-Bikes, E-Scooters & Personal Conveyances
citation: NJTR-1 Crash Report Manual (2023), Appendix: General Questions
key_points: Low-speed e-bikes, low-speed e-scooters, motorized scooters, motorized wheelchairs and hoverboards are "personal conveyances," not vehicles, for crash reporting.
Only report them on an NJTR-1 when they're in a crash with a motor vehicle in transport.
Then list the rider as a pedestrian: name, address, date of birth and sex only; select 17 – Personal Conveyance in box 108/109; describe the device in box 145.

faq.q: Do e-bike or e-scooter crashes go on an NJTR-1?
faq.a: Only when they collide with a motor vehicle in transport. A rider who falls alone or hits a fixed object isn't captured on the NJTR-1.

faq.q: How do I list the rider?
faq.a: As a pedestrian, with only name, address, date of birth and sex. Select 17 – Personal Conveyance and describe the device in the narrative.

faq.q: What is a low-speed electric bicycle?
faq.a: Two or three wheels, working pedals and a motor under 750 watts. Class 1 assists only while pedaling and stops at 20 mph. Class 2 can run on the motor alone but stops assisting at 20 mph.

faq.q: What is a low-speed electric scooter?
faq.a: A stand-up scooter with a floorboard and handlebars whose motor tops out under 19 mph.

A miniature motor vehicle without federal safety certification: pocket bikes, mini choppers, mini motorcycles, motorized skateboards and similar. They can't be ridden on public streets, highways, sidewalks or public property (except by riders with a mobility-related disability), or on private property without permission.

A self-balancing two-wheeled device under 20 mph. It may be used on roads, sidewalks and bike paths with a cyclist's rights and duties. No license, registration or insurance required. The rider must wear a helmet and be 16 or older (unless they have a mobility-related disability). Towns can regulate them. Penalties: a warning first, then a $10 fine, then impound for up to 30 days.
